Effect of surface roughness on pool boiling heat transfer at a heated
surface having moderate wettability
Jinsub Kim, Seongchul Jun, Ram Laksnarain, Seung M. You ⇑
Mechanical Engineering Department, Erik Jonsson School of Engineering and Computer Science, The University of Texas at Dallas, 800 W. Campbell Rd., Richardson, TX 75080,
United States

Keywords:

a b s t r a c t
The effect of surface roughness on pool boiling heat transfer coefficient and critical heat flux (CHF) at a
copper surface having moderate wettability was studied in saturated water. Copper surfaces were polished with sandpapers of different average surface roughness (Ra), ranging from 0.041 lm to 2.36 lm.
Test measurements included static and dynamic contact angles for each of the nine surfaces tested.
Although the surface roughness, Ra, moderately influenced the contact angles, pool boiling test results
successfully correlated with the coefficient, Csf, in the well-known Rohsenow correlation. The CHF
showed noticeably strong dependence and an enhanced performance on the surface roughness as well.
The CHF at the roughest surface (Ra = 2.36 lm) was 1625 kW/m2, which is approximately twice as much
of that at the smoothest surface (Ra = 0.041 lm). The large increase in CHF with increasing surface
roughness is considered to be a consequence of the capillary wicking from the surrounding liquid to
the dry spot. A model for the CHF is obtained by modifying an existing correlation for pool boiling with
the inclusion of the capillary wicking effect, and a comparison of the results with the experimental data
shows good agreement when the wicking effect is included in the correlation.

1. Introduction
Surface characteristics of heated surfaces are considered one of
the most dominant factors affecting boiling heat transfer. Many
researchers have studied the effect of surface roughness on the
pool boiling heat transfer since Jakob's study of its effects on pool
boiling [1]. Using rigorous experiments, Rohsenow [2] included the
surface effects in his boiling correlation by matching the surface-
fluid combination to the proper coefficient, Csf. Subsequently, many
studies have revealed the relationship between roughened surfaces
and an increase in the number of nucleation sites, resulting in augmented boiling heat transfer [3-6]. Recent research efforts are
focused on boiling heat transfer with a more complex surface
exhibiting multiscale roughness [7], surface roughness accompanying a wettability change [8], and roughness in complex geometries [9]. A few attempts have been made to develop more
accurate correlations between heat transfer coefficient h and
roughness parameters [10-12]; these correlations were tabulated
and compared with experimental data by Jones et al. [13]. Even
though there are many correlations available, based on extensive
experimentation with a variety of fluids over a range of pressures,
they do not all have a simple physical reasoning, unlike the Rohsenow correlation. Therefore, the first objective of the present study
is to understand the nucleate boiling heat transfer enhancement
due to surface roughness by establishing the relationship between
the average roughness Ra and the coefficient Csf in the conventional
Rohsenow correlation.
In contrast to the clear relation between heat transfer coefficient
and surface roughness [13], the effect of surface roughness on the
critical heat flux (CHF) is still obscure. Many researchers believed
that the CHF is triggered by the hydrodynamic instability [14]
and does not include the effect of the surface condition, viz. surface
roughness and wettability. The surface conditions were overlooked
for a long time until Ramilison et al. [15] reported that they are
important and concluded that the wettability effect on CHF is more
prominent than the roughness effect. Many other studies related to
the effect of surface roughness on the CHF were performed [16-18]
and their data showed varying augmentation of CHF with increasing surface roughness. However, the extent of the augmentation
was no more than ±20%. Although surface roughness shows somewhat limited enhancement of CHF for typical metal surfaces, recent
studies on the effect of surface roughness on hydrophilic silicon
surfaces exhibited a much larger augmentation of CHF, unlike metal
surfaces. Some researchers have focused on the combined effect of
wettability and surface micro/nanostructures on silicon surfaces.

They have treated super-hydrophilic coating on well-designed arti-
ficial microstructures. These types of microstructures were fabricated on silicon wafer surfaces because micro-fabrication on
silicon surfaces is fully developed as an accurate and mature technique. Some of these studies reported a surprisingly large increase
in CHF on super-hydrophilic structured surfaces [7,19,20]. Rahman
et al. [20] attained the CHF of as high as 2570 kW/m2 on their
hierarchically-structured silicon surface using the bio-template of
the tobacco mosaic virus. The increase seems to be beyond the limit
that can be attained by wettability alone. It is hypothesized that the
capillary wicking effect prevents dry-out of the heated surface, thus
resulting in augmented CHF. From the studies on silicon surfaces, it
is optimistic to anticipate similar results on metal surfaces provided
they are hydrophilic. O'Hanley et al. [8] pointed out that surface
conditions including wettability, roughness, and porosity should
be considered as separate parameters for precisely estimating the
effect of each parameter on CHF. The present study is intended to
start from roughened copper surfaces having moderate wettability,
which means normal copper surfaces with contact angles of
approximately 60-70 . Because it is not super-hydrophilic but still
hydrophilic, it is expected that the wettability effect is relatively
small, but capillary wicking due to the roughness change is still
effective. Simultaneously, the static and dynamic contact angles
are also measured in order to investigate the variation of contact
angles with increasing surface roughness. On the basis of the experimental data, a CHF correlation including the capillary wicking is
proposed that is appropriate for metal surfaces by using roughness
parameter Ra.
2. Experimental setup
2.1. Surface preparation and characterization
Copper blocks of size 10 mm 10 mm 3 mm were prepared
to serve as test surfaces. The top and bottom surfaces were
polished with a 600 grit sandpaper and cleaned by sonicating in
an isopropyl alcohol (IPA) solution, after which a 20-X heating element was soldered to the bottom side of the copper block. In order
to measure the temperature, a 30 AWG type T thermocouple was
inserted into a hole drilled at the center of the copper block, where
the hole is located at the 1.5 mm below the boiling surface. The top
surfaces were polished again with various sandpapers having 2000,
600, 220, and 80 grit, and a compound that was a mixture of alumina and silicon oxide nanoparticles and tallow. The compound
produced a smoother surface than that obtained by the sandpaper
polishing process. The polishing was performed in one direction,
which naturally made unidirectional scratches on the copper surfaces. The number of strokes for polishing was increased with
increasing sandpaper grit because more strokes were required for
making smoother surfaces. Although the number of strokes was
50 for the 220 and 80 grit sandpapers, it was 100 for the 600 grit
sandpaper and approximately 300 for the 2000 grit sandpaper. A
total of nine samples were prepared, two samples for each sandpaper and one for the compound.
The polished surfaces were characterized in two ways: wettability measurement and roughness measurement. Before the boiling test, the static and dynamic contact angles for each surface
were measured using a goniometer (KRUSS, DSA30). The volume
of the sessile droplet was 11.5 ll for static contact angles. For
advancing contact angles, the initial droplet of 30 ll was set up
on the surface and the volume was increased to 50 ll by feeding
water at a rate of 20 ll/min. For receding contact angles, the droplet of 50 ll at the end of the advancing process shrank to zero
volume at a rate of 20 ll/min. After the boiling test, the static
and dynamic contact angles were measured again to see how
much the angles were changed during the test. The surface
roughness was measured using the surface roughness tester
(Mitutoyo, SJ-210). The tip radius of the probe was 2 lm, the
measuring force was 0.75 mN, and the evaluation length was
4 mm. Each sample was scanned at six different points to obtain
the representative roughness. The roughness definition and the

2.2. Pool boiling test section and test procedure
Fig. 1 shows the design of the test heater used in collecting data
for the pool boiling experiments. A polished copper block bonded
with the heating element is placed on the polycarbonate substrate
and surrounded with epoxy adhesives (3M DP420) having low
thermal conductivity of 0.18 W/m K, as shown in Fig. 1. The polished top surface is exposed to the exterior and acts as a boiling
surface for the experiment. Fig. 2 shows a detailed drawing of
the test chamber used in the experiment. A Graham-type coil condenser was used to condense and return the generated vapor to the
chamber. The generated bubbles were observed through the sight
glasses situated at the front and rear sides, and a high-speed camera was installed to capture them during the experiment. The saturated liquid temperature and vapor temperature were measured
using type T thermocouple probes inserted inside the chamber. A
pressure transducer (0-172 kPa, ±0.25% accuracy) was connected
to the chamber in order to measure the internal saturation
pressure.
Approximately 2 l of distilled water was filled into the chamber
with the test heater assembly placed at the center of the test chamber. Noncondensable gas in the water was removed by boiling the
water with immersion heaters and band heaters for 1 h as a part of
the degassing process. The immersion heaters were then turned
off, but the band heaters were kept on so that the water was maintained in its saturation state. Once the liquid temperature and
internal pressure became stable, the test was initiated by applying
the specified current to the test heater. The wall temperature, liquid temperature, vapor temperature, and pressure were measured,
as well as the input current by measuring the voltage across a
shunt resistor that was connected serially with the heater in the
circuit. The input heat was calculated from the measured values
of input current and voltage drop across the test heater. Once the
wall temperature reached steady state, the current was increased
to the next specified value. The temperatures were averaged every
20 s and the steady state was considered to exist when the temperature difference was less than 0.1 C between two consecutive
average
values.

temperature by more than 20 C when compared to the value at
the previous power input. The CHF was determined to be the average of the previous steady power input and the current power
input which showed abrupt increase in wall temperature.
2.3. Uncertainty
The uncertainty analysis was performed by using the Kline and
McClintock method for single-sample experiments [21]. The uncertainty of saturation temperature (Tsat) was calculated from the
uncertainty of the pressure measurement. Because the pressure
transducer has an accuracy of ±0.25% in full range (0-172 kPa),
the uncertainty of the saturation temperature is estimated as
±0.1 K. The wall temperature was determined using the Fourier's
law for conduction through the 1.5 mm copper block from the
thermocouple location to the boiling surface. The wall temperature
(Tw) has an uncertainty of ±0.5 K. Input power, which is calculated
from the measured voltage drop and current, has an error of
±0.2 kW/m2 at q00 = 1000 kW/m2. Heat loss through the epoxy
insulation layer was estimated as 0.5% of total heat dissipation
by a simple numerical calculation. The heater area's uncertainty
was estimated as 5% of the total heated area. The uncertainty of

Rz, as defined by the ISO standards, is the average of the five highest
peaks and five deepest valleys. Sm refers to the mean spacing
between peaks. Sm can provide information in the transverse direction, which is important for estimating the number of scratches per
unit width. In some studies, a minimum height or a minimum depth
is employed for ignoring small peaks, but in the present study no
restriction was placed in counting the peaks. Because boiling heat
transfer is related to the length scale of the heated surface, Ra was
chosen as the representative roughness parameter in this study.
The average roughness increased from 0.041 lm for the surface polished with compound to 2.36 lm for the surface polished with the
80 grit sandpaper. SEM images in Fig. 3 clearly show the different
structures of the tested surfaces. The height (or the depth) of the
unidirectional scratches increased with increasing Ra, whereas the

case of the smoothest surface of Ra = 0.041 lm (compound) the
number of scratches also decreased, which means it had only sparse

the number of scratches because Sm is inversely proportional to the
number of scratches. It increases with increasing roughness from

Both the static and dynamic contact angles were measured for
all nine surfaces. The unidirectional scratches require two different
viewing angles for measuring the contact angles: parallel to the
scratches and normal to the scratches. Fig. 4 depicts the sessile
drops captured in the two directions for the representative surface
with Ra = 0.169 lm (600 grit #1). The contact angles captured parallel to the scratches normally have higher values because the
movement of contact lines is limited by the contact line pinning
effect [22]. In contrast, the contact angles captured normal to the
scratches showed lower values as the sessile drops spread easily
through the scratches. Contact angles were measured before the
boiling tests as well as after in order to investigate how much
the contact angles changed during the tests. Static contact angles
of all nine surfaces captured in the two directions are shown in
Fig. 5. Static angles in the parallel direction, measured before the
boiling tests, show only a slight increase with Ra, approximately
70 . The static contact angles in the normal direction are lower
than those in the parallel direction because of the pinning and
spreading effects, respectively, in those directions. It is noticeable
that the static angle in the normal direction decreases with
increasing roughness. This means that the spreading through the
scratches increases as the surface becomes rougher. Because the
spreading is caused by the capillary wicking, it can be inferred that
the capillary wicking effect is increased with increasing surface
roughness. Hence, the final averages of static contact angles in both
directions have limited variation according to the surface roughness because of the opposing tendencies between contact line pinning in the parallel direction and spreading in the normal direction.

tests are the same as those before the boiling tests, but contact
angles at both directions were increased by 5-15 for all surfaces.
The increase of the contact angles during the boiling tests is
thought to result from the oxidation of the copper surfaces even
at low temperatures near 100 C [23].
The dynamic contact angles (advancing and receding contact
angles) were also measured as shown in Fig. 6, where the dynamic
contact angles for the surface with Ra = 0.169 lm (600 grit #1) are
shown. Although the advancing contact angle is nearly constant
throughout the growth period of the droplet, the receding contact
angle exhibits a monotonic decrease during most of the shrinkage
period of the droplet as a result of the contact line pinning effect.
Because the receding of the triple contact line occurs only near
the end of the shrinkage period, the receding contact angles were
evaluated for only 5 s after the contact line actually moved. The
advancing and receding contact angles with regard to Ra are shown
in Fig. 7. The trend of the advancing contact angles with Ra is similar to that of the static contact angles except for somewhat higher
values by approximately 10-15 . The receding contact angles also
show a similar trend to the static contact angles, but they have
much lower values of approximately 10 compared with the static
contact angles. The variation of the receding contact angles according to Ra was not large, which implies negligible CHF variation with
increasing Ra because the CHF is believed to be closely related to
the receding contact angle [24]. This is why a large variation of
CHF with Ra, which is observed later in the pool boiling curves, cannot be explained solely by the wettability effect.
Boiling curves for all the tested surfaces having different roughness are shown in Fig. 8. It is clearly demonstrated that the boiling
curve shifts to the left as Ra increases, which indicates better nucleate boiling heat transfer performance with increasing Ra. This is
consistent with previous studies that dealt with the effect of surface roughness on nucleate boiling heat transfer [4,6,25]. However,
the change in CHF with increasing Ra in Fig. 8 is considerably large.
The CHF was merely 775 kW/m2 at the smoothest surface of
Ra = 0.041 lm, whereas CHF at the roughest surface of Ra = 2.36 lm
was as much as 1625 kW/m2, which is more than the double of
that at the smoothest surface. Therefore, the effects of surface
roughness on nucleate boiling heat transfer and CHF must be
investigated more thoroughly.

Although Csf is a function of contact angle as well as surface
roughness, Eq. (10) is likely to be applicable to surfaces having
moderate wettability similar to the surfaces tested in the present
study. A more generalized and complete correlation of Csf should
be acquired through further studies on the roughness effect for
various wetting surfaces.
The boiling curves in Fig. 8 exhibit significant changes of the
CHF with surface roughness. Many researchers have simply
reported this behavior as augmentation of CHF due to surface
roughness. However, the extent of augmentation demonstrated
by the experimental data shows large differences according to
the surface type, such as metal surfaces or silicon wafer surfaces.
CHF variation with changing roughness on the metal surfaces has
been reported to be approximately 10-20% in general [15,18]. In
contrast, recent studies on CHF enhancement with silicon wafer
surfaces show much larger augmentations with increasing roughness factor r, where roughness factor r is defined as the ratio of
the actual contact area to the projected area [7,19,26,27].
Table 2 summarizes various studies regarding the effect of surface roughness on CHF for both metal surfaces and silicon wafer
surfaces. CHF enhancement for metal surfaces is at most 10-20%
except for the data measured by Ferjancˇicˇ and Golobicˇ [28] for
etched surfaces, which exhibited approximately a 50% enhancement. Surfaces polished with sandpapers normally showed a
10-20% increase in CHF, whereas surfaces etched in diluted acid
exhibited larger enhancements, as much as 51%. In contrast, the

enhancement of CHF on silicon wafer surfaces is more pronounced
and shows more than a 100% increase in CHF, depending on the
roughness factor, r. The considerably higher enhancement of CHF
on the silicon surfaces can be attributed to the increased capillary
wicking phenomenon with increasing surface roughness. Moreover, because most silicon surfaces were super-hydrophilic, aided
by the nanostructures, it is believed that capillary wicking is more
intensive in the microgeometries on the silicon surfaces. Because
capillary pressure exists if the surface is hydrophilic, the copper
surfaces having moderate wettability in the present study certainly
have the capillary wicking effect.

decrease with increasing Ra because of the capillary wicking (Figs. 5
and 7). Fig. 11 shows the model of a hovering bubble on the
modified surface structures created by the current surface roughness following the original model proposed by Haramura and Katto
[29]. They explained that CHF occurs at the dry-out when the liquid
sublayer beneath the hovering bubble completely evaporates. In
the case of a perfectly smooth surface, the liquid amount in the liquid sublayer is established at the initial stage of the bubble cycle
without any additional supply. However, for roughened surfaces,
adjacent liquid is likely to be transported to the sublayer by capillary wicking. This additional liquid supply could delay the dry-out
of the liquid sublayer at the same q00 where CHF occurs at the perfectly smooth surface, thus augmenting the CHF at the roughened
surface. Because the capillary wicking increases further with surface roughness, the augmentation of CHF is predicted to increase
as well. The CHF measurements in the present study clearly
demonstrate this fact with CHF increasing from 775 kW/m2 at the
smoothest surface (Ra = 0.041 lm) to 1625 kW/m2 at the roughest
surface (Ra = 2.36 lm).
The CHF model, including the wettability effect on the conventional hydrodynamic model, was first proposed by Kandlikar [24].
He successfully added the wettability effect in his CHF model by
balancing momentum change due to evaporation with the gravity
and surface tension forces exerted on the bubble. Recently, some
researchers considered the contribution of surface roughness to
CHF as an additional term to Kandlikar's CHF model. Ahn et al.
[19] ascribed the large increase of CHF on their super-hydrophilic
surfaces to the existence of additional liquid spreading above the
wettability effect. This liquid spreading is thought to be another
expression of capillary wicking. As shown in Table 2, Chu et al.
[7] modified the Kandlikar correlation to accommodate the effect
of surface roughness by changing cos h to r cos h, where r is the
roughness factor. Kim et al. [27] also proposed a CHF correlation
including the surface roughness effect by adding a capillary wicking term to the Kandlikar model. Although various attempts were
made to fit the capillary effect into the CHF model for explaining
the large augmentation on silicon surfaces, an appropriate CHF correlation accounting for the roughness effect on metal surfaces is
difficult to analyze. Because a different roughness parameter r is
normally used for silicon surfaces, a new correlation using Ra is
required to account for the roughness effect on CHF for metal
surfaces.
For CHF modeling on the present metal surfaces, it can be
thought of as having many small capillary tubes beneath the vapor
bubble as shown in Fig. 12. Force balance between momentum
change due to evaporation and forces acting on the vapor bubble
can then be analyzed in a similar way to Kandlikar's original
approach, with an additional capillary force term. Quan et al.
[30] first considered capillary wicking due to surface roughness
as an additional force term in the force balance equation:

In the present study, the accommodation factor S and the constant C were obtained from Eq. (26) using the measured data-contact angles, roughness parameters (Ra and Sm), and CHFs. The static
contact angles captured in the parallel and normal directions to the
scratches were averaged at all roughened surfaces. The averaged
static contact angle, which was calculated to be 64.5 , is employed
for the calculation of S and C because the average at each surface
showed similar values within ±5 . The S and C values are found
to be 0.811 and 87.8 for the current data set. The current value
of accommodation factor S, 0.811, is almost identical to the value
of 0.823 suggested by Ahn et al. [19]. As a result, the curves calculated from the final CHF correlation (Eq. (26)) at different contact
angles (10 , 30 , 50 , and 70 ) exhibited a trend with increasing
surface roughness at different wettability in Fig. 13. The present
data are also plotted in the figure with the relevant curve obtained
at 64.5 , the average static contact angle measured in the present
study. The data show good agreement with the correlation, with
a mean absolute error of 4.1%. Fig. 13 also indicates the possibility
of attaining higher CHF than 2500 kW/m2 at the super-hydrophilic
roughened surfaces (h = 10 and 30 in the figure). Additional studies on super-hydrophilic and hydrophobic metal surfaces would
give us full understandings of the combined effect of roughness
and wettability on CHF in boiling heat transfer.
4. Conclusions
The effect of surface roughness on the nucleate boiling heat
transfer and CHF at copper surfaces having moderate contact
angles in pool boiling of saturated water was investigated. The
average roughness Ra was varied from 0.041 lm to 2.36 lm, and
static and dynamic contact angles were measured before and after
each boiling test for all nine surfaces. From the test results and discussion, the following conclusions are deduced.
Both static and dynamic contact angles for tested surfaces
showed similar behavior with increasing surface roughness.
The contact angles viewed in the parallel direction tend to
increase with Ra, while the contact angles viewed in the normal
direction tend to decrease with Ra. This behavior is considered
to result from the contact line pinning (parallel direction) and
capillary wicking (normal direction).
It was confirmed that surface roughness enhances nucleate
boiling heat transfer because of the increased number of active
nucleation sites. For a boiling surface having moderate wettability, coefficient Csf in the Rohsenow correlation was successfully
correlated with regard to the dimensionless average roughness.
The heat transfer coefficient calculated from the proposed correlation shows good agreement with the experimental data.
CHF exhibited considerable augmentation with increasing surface roughness. It increased from 775 kW/m2 at the smoothest
surface (Ra = 0.041 lm) to 1625 kW/m2 at the roughest surface
(Ra = 2.36 lm). The large augmentation is believed to result
from capillary wicking on the roughened surface. An appropriate CHF correlation including the capillary wicking effect was
proposed for metal surfaces and it showed good agreement
with the experimental data (average 4% difference).
